newsitem.title: JAPAN: Strike at Norilsk may spark palladium supply fears.
newsitem.headline: Strike at Norilsk may spark palladium supply fears.

text.p: Japanese palladium and platinum traders said on Thursday that a possible strike at Russian producer Norilsk Nickel NKEL.RTS could spark global supply fears for platinum group metals.

The possibility of a prolonged strike at a major world supplier, coupled with lingering uncertainty over the fate of the Japan-Russia talks on 1997 platinum and palladium supplies, was enough to trigger speculative buying, they said.

On Wednesday, a Norilsk Nickel management spokesman played down talk that its trade union was considering a strike on March 15 over salary and other arrears, saying an independent arbitration court was examining the workers' complaints.
Japanese traders said that a strike at Norilsk is unlikely to immediately affect Russian exports as Russian producers are believed to have sufficient stocks to meet near-term demand.

"Russia is believed to have ample palladium stocks, although platinum stocks may be running down," one trader at a major trading house said. "Even if a strike takes place, it would not have an significant impact on Russian supplies for the near term."
Norilsk is a major world supplier of cobalt, nickel and platinum group metals. Russia accounts for about 60 percent of world palladium supplies.
Japanese traders said they were not worried about talk that Russian platinum stocks may be dwindling, because South Africa is also a leading producer of platinum.
On Wednesday, spot palladium was fixed in London at $150.00 an ounce, its highest level since August 22.
Those gains were extended further in Asia's Thursday trade, when spot palladium quotes quotes soared to $155/$156.
Meanwhile, annual Japan-Russia talks on platinum group metals, usually held in mid-December, have been postponed indefinitely due mainly to problems with Russia's budget.

Reflecting the suspension of Russian exports, supplies of palladium sponge, a form of the metal used in catalytic converters for cars, were extremely tight, while there were relatively sufficient inventories of palladium ingot, which is used mainly in electronic components, traders said.
Premiums in Japan for palladium sponge were quoted at $5 to $7 per ounce over the world benchmark, while premiums for palladium ingot were quoted at a more normal $1 to $2.

An official at a Japanese bullion house said the recent rallies in platinum and palladium were driven by speculators, and the rise in yen-based prices of platinum group metals slowed physical business.
"Electronic appliance manufacturers will tend to shift to cheaper metals if palladium prices rise too much," he said.
Russian supplies to Japan have been halted since the beginning of the year but palladium ingot inventories were built up during heavy Russian sales in the spot market in late 1996, traders said.
Japan is the world's largest consumer of platinum and palladium.
